newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish markets spooked by fresh inflation fears.
newsitem.headline: Turkish markets spooked by fresh inflation fears.

text.p: Turkish bond prices rocketed by around eight percentage points while shares were dragged lower on Wednesday after a minister in the new right-left coalition stoked fears of triple-digit inflation, brokers said.

Economy minister Gunes Taner said on Tuesday he expected year-on-year inflation to reach around 100 percent by the end of 1997 compared to a forecast of 85 percent made earlier by the three-week-old coalition government.

"Although the market was expecting the central bank to raise money market rates because of the rising cost of funding in the bond market, the minister's words on inflation were a surprise for us," said a private bank treasurer.

Taner's comments, made in an interview with Reuters, sparked a transfer of funds from the stock market to bonds. The most active May 13, 1997 paper jumped 7.6 percentage points to 119.09 percent from 111.50 at the close on Tuesday.
The IMKB National-100 share index ended the morning session down 41 points, or 2.1 percent, at 1,912. Trading volume slipped to 7.9 trillion lira ($48 million) from 9.5 trillion on Tuesday.
"The statements by Gunes Taner are creating an excuse for speculators," said Selim Basar of Gedik Securities.
He said recent public offerings were at the heart of the stock market weakness. "They withdrew a significiant amount of cash from the stock market," Basar said.
Taner told Reuters the previous Islamist-led coalition's economic policies had destabilised domestic markets and this would lead to higher inflation in the second half.
"As a result, inflation began to rise rapidly and we think the trend will continue and year-end inflation will be around 100 percent," Taner said.

Financial markets had welcomed the new government, which replaced a troubled alliance between Islamists and conservatives who were edged out of office under pressure from the country's secularist establishment.
The Turkish central bank raised its money market rates by one to two percentage points at the opening on Wednesday. Overnight rates jumped to 54-74 pct from the previous 52-72 percent.
The lira fell to 157,400 against the dollar from 156,310 on Tuesday after firming at the opening to 156,900.
Brokers said the downside for shares was limited.
"The market came up against solid selling," said broker Ibrahim Donmez of Yasar Investment. "But despite this there are shares with a firm basis. There will be reaction buying at 1,900 points."
Strongest declines were posted by the tourism sector which fell 4.16 percent. Trading was heaviest in flat steel producer Eregli, Turkish Airlines and the C series shares of T. Is Bank.

Taner said a primary task of the new right-left coalition was to tackle the budget deficit, which the previous government aimed to balance and is expected to reach 2,500 trillion lira ($15.9 billion) in 1997 as a whole.
"What we have done immediately was to raise taxes and prices on various goods. But with all those rises we cannot finance all of the budget deficit. We have to borrow from the domestic market."

Taner said the government would also tap foreign markets for borrowing and said it planned privatisations of $12 billion for the first half of 1998 following targeted sell-offs of $4 billion this year.
He said the appointment of the new government had brought confidence in local and international markets.
"There is a rebounding in markets and confidence for Turkey has begun to rise again," he said.
($1 = 157,400 Turkish lira)
